title: Distributed upcycling of mixed plastic wastes: material challenges and opportunities for additive manufacturing.
text:
Highlights

Evaluation of a distributed upcycling approach to process multi-material post-consumer plastic waste using open-source additive manufacturing (AM) technologies.
Identification of the role of material compatibilizers in enhancing the properties of rPET and rHDPE blends using two distinct processing methods: conventional extrusion-injection molding and large-scale FGF 3D printing.

Purpose: The purpose of this study is to present the evaluation of a distributed upcycling approach to process multi-material post-consumer plastic waste using open-source additive manufacturing (AM) technologies. More precisely, the study aims to assess the technical feasibility and print quality of using mixed plastic wastes as a feedstock for AM mapping the role of material compatibilizers.
Materials and methods: Post-consumer water bottles where collected from Nancy (France) and Kirkland (Canada). The composition is approximately 90 wt% PET (body) and 10 wt%. HDPE (cap). The bottles were shredded and re-granulated to produce a feedstock for additive manufacturing. Moreover, Kraton G-1650 and G-1652 by Kraton Polymers (Almere, Netherlands) were used as non-reactive compatibilizers. Both are linear SEBS copolymer including about 30 wt% of polystyrene units. Additionally, a maleated SEBS cirKular + C1010 (C1010) by Univar Solutions (France) was used as a reactive compatiblizer. C1010 contains ~1.5% of grafted maleic anhydride. Blending and samples preparation were prepared in a co-rotating twin screw extruder and 3D printed using an open source large-format fused granular fabrication printer. Compounding process using a co-rotating twin-screw micro-compounder (DSM Xplore Instrument, Netherlands) and injection molding machine (DSM Xplore Instrument, Netherlands) was used as reference. On the other hand, the printing process was implemented using a modified open-source FGF printer with three heat zones (Gigabot XL re:3D, Houston, TX, USA). For all the ternary blends the quantity of compatibilizer utilized was 10 wt%. The mechanical properties of the printed parts were evaluated through tensile testing. Thermal, morphological and rehological characterizaion of the samples was performed.
Results and Discussion: This study highlights the role of compatibilizers in enhancing the properties of rPET and rHDPE blends using two distinct processing methods: conventional extrusion-injection molding and large-scale FGF 3D printing. The results showed that the compatibilizers improves phase interaction, increasing the elongation at break by ~40 %, enhancing rheological behavior by reducing the MFI between 10 % and 47 %, depending on the compatibilizer used, and improving the morphological properties in reference samples. In contrast, printed samples exhibited less degradation and a more crystalline structure at elevated temperatures, as confirmed by FTIR and DSC-TGA analyses. However, the mechanical properties of the printed samples were ~50 % inferior than those of the EI, primarily due to suboptimal layer adhesion, void formation, and insufficient material homogenization.
Conclusions and perspectives: Distributed upcycling offers a pathway to reduce manufacturing costs by transforming plastic waste into 3D printing feedstock. While compounding process remains a well-established technology, the direct 3D printing process still faces challenges in achieving consistent material properties. The single-screw extrusion mechanism of the FGF printer limits blend homogenization and reduces compatibilizer effectiveness. Nevertheless, this approach holds promise for recycling multimaterial blends and can be optimized through more reliable printing methods, including the implementation of a twin-screw or planetary roller extruder to enhance blend homogenization. Additionally, refining printing parameters adapted to the compatibilizers could further enhance the mechanical properties and consistency of printed objects. Future work should also investigate the recyclability of printed materials over multiple cycles, assess the environmental and economical feasibility of using FGF to process post-consumer plastic waste. Expanding this approach to other common plastics such as PP, LDPE, PS could expand its applicability of this method. This would require re-optimizing the compatibilizer system and adjusting printing parameters to account for the different processing behaviors of these polymers.

title: Research
text:
See on the Website of ERPI

At the ERPI laboratory (https://erpi.univ-lorraine.fr/) of the Universiré de Lorraine, one major interest is the the development of methodologies, tools and case studies in the area of innovation process management. From engineering and design and territorial perspectives, the laboratory has been developing research on the intersection of additive manufacturing, circular economy and urban manufacturing.
One of the research axis concerns the intersection on three major societal issues as follows:

The circular economy of plastics as disruptor paradigm in political, industrial and societal perspective (De Pascale et al. 2023; Ramli et al. 2024),
The development of open design (Bakırlıoğlu and Kohtala 2019; Pacheco et al. 2025) including the open source technology as alternative approach of traditional technology development and,
The experimental development of the urban manufacturing approaches (Herrmann et al. 2020; Ijassi et al. 2025) (i.e. Fablabs, Tiers Lieux, Recycleries and Matériauthèque) that usually are grassroot mouvements. These approaches are reframing the manufacturing networks at a local level and can give perspective on eco-innovation process for circular economy (Kasmi et al. 2021).



See for instance the LAUDS Factories EU Project 
Indeed, current centralized waste management systems remain structurally inadequate (Lerpiniere et al. 2025) to address the complex and systemic nature of plastic pollution, a crisis that increasingly threatens planetary boundaries (Villarrubia-Gómez et al. 2024) and the safe operating space for humanity.
In this regard, ERPI Laboratory have been developing the concept of “distributed recycling via additive manufacturing (DRAM)” (Cruz Sanchez et al. 2020) as illustrated in Figure 1. It involves the technical feasibility of using recycled plastics into the additive manufacturing printing process chain. Particularly, the use systems based on material extrusion which are the most used in industry and general public.






Figure 1: Distributed recycling via additive manufacturing developed at the ERPI Laboratory



The Recovery (I) phase addresses the logistical operations required to collect plastic waste for reuse within DRAM systems. The Preparation (II) phase encompasses the identification, separation, sorting, size reduction, and cleaning of plastic waste to ensure adequate quality. The Compounding (III) phase focuses on the development of mono- and composite materials. After, the Feedstock (IV) phase focuses on producing materials suitable for printing, either in filament form for FFF or as particles for FGF. The Printing (V) phase addresses application development and process optimization for recycled materials. Finally, the Quality (VI) phase involves multi-level technical characterization of recycled materials and printed parts.
Therefore, three major scales are simultaneaosly studied, as illustrated in Figure 1 :

Material level: The study of strategies for post-consumer plastic recycling/upcycling to enhance the structural properties of plastic waste.
Process level: Open-source hardware (i.e additive manufacturing, manual injection, sheetpress etc) as a promising pathway to transform plastic waste into usable artifacts/products.
Socio-technical level: Urban manufacturing systems can provide a conducive environment for distributed upcycling, enabling the transformation of plastic waste into locally relevant products, closer to where the waste is generated.

For instance, using desktop-scale fused filament fabrication (FFF) (Cruz Sanchez et al. 2014) and fused granular fabrication (FGF) (Alexandre et al. 2020), we have demonstrated their potential as technical enablers for the mechanical recycling of mono-thermoplastic waste, such as polylactic acid (PLA), from material (Cruz et al. 2015; Cruz Sanchez et al. 2017), process (Cruz Sanchez et al. 2014; Alexandre et al. 2020), and socio-technical perspectives (Santander et al. 2020; Caceres-Mendoza et al. 2023). Recently, the work on multi-material (Suescun Gonzalez et al. 2024; Gonzalez et al. 2025) have openend new explorative paths that aims to see the upcycling (Riondet et al. 2022) potential of this approach.




The incompatibility between different plastic types—due to variations in chemical and molecular structures—remains a major limitation, leading to poor interfacial adhesion and low material performance (Kassab et al. 2023).
Our aim in UP3DCYCLING is to fully develop an upcycling strategy targeting plastics that are sorted but not recycled due to the lack of viable value chains.
In this sense our mission is to investigate the mechanical upcycling of mixed plastic waste through the incorporation of compatibilizers during the melting process.
design catalysts but always considering their scalability. Our main outcome of is a comprehensive benchmarking of compatibilization strategies applied to the six primary single-use plastics: polyethylene terephthalate (PET), high density polyethylene (HDPE), polypropylene (PP), low density polyethylene (LDPE), polystyrene (PS) and polylactic acid (PLA).
The ambition is to establish a systematic framework defining minimum quality standards for additive manufacturing using blended recycled materials—an area that remains underdeveloped in current research.





Logo of UP3Dcycling








The use of open source additive manufacturing (aka 3D Printing) is revolutionizing the manner that plastics could be processed and transformed. In spite of the great promise of additive manufacturing as an advanced form of future manufacturing, there are still fundamental challenges with respect to sustainability that need to be addressed.
Some of the material needs for additive manufacturing include sustainable sources of printing inks, resins, and filaments, as well as pathways for polymer recycling, upcycling, and chemical circularity.



Logo of UP3Dcycling











Urban Manufacturing




UP3DCYCLING aims to explore distributed upcycling from a Design for Sustainability (DfS) perspective (Ceschin and Gaziulusoy 2019), focusing on its socio-technical implications. The project will adopt a mixed qualitative and quantitative approach to analyze urban upcycling systems.
Previous research studies have explored distributed recycling through life-cycle assessment (kerdlap2020?; kerdlap2022?), the broader implications of distributed upcycling as a sustainability transition remain insufficiently understood (Eising-Mertsch et al. 2024).
Finally, a participatory action research approach will be implemented through a real-world case study at the ‘Green Fablab’ in Nancy https://erpi.univ-lorraine.fr/projet/green-fablab/, developed since 2017 in close collaboration with local stakeholders, notably within the associative third place Octroi Nancy https://www.octroi-nancy.fr/. Within this framework, we will design and deploy an integrated workflow to collect, clean, sort, shred, and transform post-consumer plastic waste into new products via additive manufacturing, enabling the local valorization of materials currently excluded from conventional recycling systems (Cruz Sanchez et al. 2020; Santander et al. 2020; Caceres-Mendoza et al. 2023).

title: Exploring the applicability of the Open Source Technology Readiness Levels (OSTRL) framework to circular economy practices in LAUDS Factories
text:
Opening Frame
In recent years the advancement of digital communities make possible the development of an open design approach, becoming source for product innovation instead of conventional and proprietary product development (Shi and Jiang 2025; Bakırlıoğlu and Kohtala 2019). Aiming at a ‘design global / manufacturing local’ (Kostakis et al. 2018) seems a proto-industrialization (Sabel and Zeitlin 1985) transition that is taking place in urban settlements that could a major impact in the next short future.  The Open Source Appropriate Technology (OSAT)(Pearce et al. 2010) and peer-to-peer (P2P)(Kostakis 2013) approaches have been seen potential drivers to propose an alternative globalisation manufacturing paradigm (Heikkinen 2020). Indeed, open-design can be defined as ’the state of a design project where both the process and the sources of its outputs are accessible and (re)usable, by anyone and for any purpose’(Boisseau et al. 2018). In that sense, open design make it possible the development of small-scale, economically affordable, decentralised, energy-efficient, environmentally sound technologies that could easily utilized by local communities to meet their needs (pearce2012b?; Pacheco et al. 2025). This approach have been valuable for software development because free and open source software (FOSS) providing: i) diversification and open innovation (colombo2014?), ii) cumulative innovation (boudreau2016?), iii) development efficiency (Hienerth et al. 2014), iv) organizational innovation (Alexy et al. 2013), v) higher technical quality of code (soderberg2015?), vi) encourages creativity (martinez2015?) and vii) perhaps most importantly, it avoids redundant work (Årdal and Røttingen 2016). Likewise, scientific equipement to reduce the cost with equal of quality (pearce2014k?; Pearce 2016), and having implication in national level (Pearce 2022). By relying on local resources, materials, and competencies, these approaches often challenge conventional product development models, including product functions and consumption patterns. An open source technodiversity could be a strong breakthrough contribution to sustainability and CE than traditional manufacturing paradigms to foster the creation of urban closed-loop supply chains inside urban settlements.
According the Open Source Hardware Association, the development of open hardware defines :

Hardware whose design is made publicly available so that anyone can study, modify, distribute, make, and sell the design or hardware based on that design. The hardware’s source, the design from which it is made, is available in the preferred format for making modifications to it. Ideally, open source hardware uses readily-available components and materials, standard processes, open infrastructure, unrestricted content, and open-source design tools to maximize the ability of individuals to make and use hardware. Open source hardware gives people the freedom to control their technology while sharing knowledge and encouraging commerce through the open exchange of designs

However, one major question remains. As OS hardware matures from a largely hobbyist-driven activity to a professional form of technological development:

How can be mapped the maturity level of the artifacts that are issue from an open desing approach?.
What are the observable traces that make explain the evolution of the design towards a complete openess ?, and
In what extent open-source (OS) technologies could be synergic support of sustainable and circular economy (CE) practices, especially in urban manufacturing contexts.

While OS hardware has been shown to offer over 90% cost savings for research equipment and fosters increased innovation within national economies [heikkinen2020], the absence of robust methodologies to assess the real-world implementation of OS technologies in CE contexts remains challenging, especially considering readiness, transferability, and maturity. Although several evaluation frameworks exist, e.g., material circularity index, most focus on environmental or system-level perspectives, often limiting practitioners (makers, tier-places) and researchers working on real-world OS technologies.
The main purpose of this chapter is to ..


Key concepts & Framework
Urban manufacturing (Herrmann et al. 2020; Juraschek 2022; Herrmann et al. 2019) is increasingly seen as a pathway to re-localize production through cleaner and more sustainable processes. Customised products to be produced in regions close to the consumer that create a virtuous cycle based on design-produce-use-repair-recycle loops may alternative paths resource scarcity, circularity (Sajadieh et al. 2022). This decentralized approach contrast with the current mass manufacturing paradigm are often globalized value chains products. The mass production system, in the lens of a deep transition framework, is the fruit of a complex co-evolution of single unit productions and interconnected systems (Kanger et al. 2022). However, several forms of environmental degradation have been intensified without fully assuring the social foundation’s minimum standards (e.g. healthcare, energy, water etc) (Raworth 2017).
To support their continuous adoption, the establishment the OS Technology Readiness Levels (OSTRL) framework is aims to establish a a technological blueprint in the development. OSTRL was originally developed to translate readiness into OS contexts, facilitating the assessment and development of openness in OS technologies. This project aims to refine the OSTRL framework and extend its use by testing its applicability within CE contexts beyond DRAM ecosystems. Following a practice-oriented approach, the proposal involves potential target users in evaluating real-world OS projects using OSTRLs and collecting structured feedback on their clarity, usability, and limitations. The OSTRLs are refined accordingly, and complementary uses with CE-focused assessment frameworks are evaluated for real-world adoption.


Methods & Tools

Explanation of OSTRL
Explanation of the Workshops (LAUDS consortium + Students)



LUADS in Practice

The starting activity is a structured workshop organized within the Horizon 2020 LAUDS project (https://lauds.eu/) meeting hosted at ERPI (Fall 2026). Researchers, project partners, and practitioners will apply OSTRLs to selected CE-related case studies from LAUDS through guided activities. The feedback collected during the workshop, together with further feedback at ERPI during the visiting period, will be used to refine the OSTRLs, improving their clarity and applicability. The expected outcomes include: an updated, tested version of the OSTRLs; refined use guidelines and documentation; and additional case studies as examples of OSTRL use. These elements will be included in a peer-reviewed publication and OS repositories for open dissemination and future follow-up.

Distributed upcycling of mixed plastic wastes: material, process, and socio-technical challenges
text:
Our Aim
Our overall research aims is to study, implement, and evaluate the upcycling potential of mixed plastic waste via in-situ reactive compatibilization using open-source additive manufacturing.

title: Ethnographic Analysis of Urban Manufacturing Ecosystems
text: Table 1: Overview of the internship at the ERPI Laboratory

title: Ethnographic Analysis of Urban Manufacturing Ecosystems
text:
Objective of the Internship
The internship takes place at an exploratory stage of the project, ahead of the in-depth ethnographic fieldwork in Nancy that will be carried out as part of a PhD (starting end of 2027). Its main goals are:

To map the actors, networks and public action frameworks shaping citizen-led plastic upcycling in urban manufacturing settings, from the Nancy area (local waste governance, metropolitan authority, waste collection, reuse and repair organizations, public support for third places) to regional and national networks.
To build an analytical framework and a first set of contrasts that will help situate the Nancy case (Green Fablab, Octroi Nancy third place) in the subsequent fieldwork.

title: Ethnographic Analysis of Urban Manufacturing Ecosystems
text:
Deliverable

A mapping report of the actors, networks and public action frameworks relevant to distributed plastic upcycling, from the Nancy area to the national level.
A scientific document presenting the analytical framework, the methodology and the first results, as a basis for the PhD fieldwork.
